subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 38-year-old woman of Black race presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pressure. Pelvic examination shows an enlarged uterus with an irregular, nodular contour. Ultrasound reveals several well-circumscribed myometrial masses.
question: Which of the following best describes these masses?

options.text: Malignant endometrial tumors with confluent glands
Benign myometrial tumors (fibroids) with whorled smooth muscle bundles
Endometrial tissue outside the uterus forming chocolate cysts
Fibrous adhesions within the endometrial cavity
Endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium producing a boggy uterus

explanation_correct: Leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign tumors of the myometrium and are the most common gynecologic tumor, arising in reproductive-age women with increased incidence in the Black population. They are typically multiple and classified as submucosal, intramural, or subserosal. They can cause abnormal bleeding, pelvic pressure/pain, and reproductive dysfunction. Histology shows whorled bundles of smooth muscle with well-demarcated borders, and the uterus has a nodular contour on exam.

explanation_incorrect.A: Malignant endometrial tumors with confluent glands describe endometrioid carcinoma, not a benign nodular myometrial mass.
explanation_incorrect.C: Endometrial tissue outside the uterus forming chocolate cysts is endometriosis, which does not produce a nodular myometrial tumor.
explanation_incorrect.D: Fibrous adhesions within the endometrial cavity are intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome), not myometrial masses.
explanation_incorrect.E: Endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium producing a boggy, diffusely enlarged uterus is adenomyosis, which lacks the nodular contour of discrete fibroids.

educationalObjective: Leiomyomas are benign, often multiple myometrial fibroids with whorled smooth muscle and a nodular uterus, common in reproductive-age Black women.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 32-year-old woman has a known uterine leiomyoma. She notes that the mass seems to enlarge during pregnancy and around her menses, and her doctor mentions it will likely shrink after menopause.
question: Which of the following best explains this behavior?

options.text: The tumor is driven by unopposed progesterone from chronic anovulation
The tumor is an endometrioid carcinoma that responds to tamoxifen
The tumor is composed of endometrial stroma that sheds each cycle
The tumor is estrogen sensitive, growing with high estrogen states and regressing after menopause
The tumor is an inflammatory mass that fluctuates with infection

explanation_correct: Leiomyomas are estrogen-sensitive tumors. Their size increases with elevated estrogen states such as pregnancy and before menstruation, and decreases after menopause when estrogen production falls. This hormonal responsiveness reflects estrogen and progesterone receptors on the smooth muscle cells.

explanation_incorrect.A: Unopposed progesterone from anovulation drives endometrial hyperplasia; leiomyomas are classically described as estrogen sensitive, growing in pregnancy and shrinking after menopause.
explanation_incorrect.B: Endometrioid carcinoma is a malignant endometrial tumor associated with unopposed estrogen; it is not the estrogen-sensitive benign myometrial mass described.
explanation_incorrect.C: Endometrial stroma that sheds each cycle describes normal endometrium or adenomyosis, not a discrete myometrial fibroid.
explanation_incorrect.E: An inflammatory mass fluctuating with infection would suggest a tubo-ovarian or pelvic inflammatory process, not a hormone-responsive fibroid.

educationalObjective: Leiomyomas are estrogen sensitive: they enlarge in pregnancy/high-estrogen states and regress after menopause.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with painless vaginal bleeding. Endometrial biopsy shows malignant endometrial glands growing in a back-to-back confluent pattern without intervening stroma. She has a history of obesity and long-standing unopposed estrogen exposure.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Endometrioid carcinoma of the endometrium
Benign endometrial hyperplasia without atypia
Endometriosis with chocolate cyst formation
Cervical squamous cell carcinoma
Intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome)

explanation_correct: Endometrial carcinoma is the most common gynecologic cancer in resource-rich countries and typically arises in postmenopausal women, who present with abnormal uterine bleeding. The endometrioid subtype is the most common and is associated with long-term unopposed estrogen exposure (obesity, nulliparity, anovulation). Histology shows confluent endometrial glands without intervening stroma.

explanation_incorrect.B: Endometrial hyperplasia is a premalignant proliferation of glands but lacks the confluent, back-to-back invasive glandular pattern of carcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.C: Endometriosis is benign ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus and would not show malignant confluent glands on biopsy.
explanation_incorrect.D: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma arises at the transformation zone of the cervix, not from endometrial glands, and would not arise from the endometrium.
explanation_incorrect.E: Asherman syndrome is fibrous intrauterine adhesions causing decreased menses, not a malignant glandular proliferation.

educationalObjective: Endometrial carcinoma (most commonly endometrioid) is the most common gynecologic cancer in resource-rich countries, arises in postmenopausal women with unopposed estrogen, and shows confluent glands without stroma.
source: Generated from 15. Reproductive.pdf - Pathology: Uterine conditions: neoplastic (leiomyoma, endometrial carcinoma)

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 67-year-old woman with a history of obesity and nulliparity undergoes endometrial biopsy for postmenopausal bleeding. The pathologist describes malignant endometrial glands arranged in a confluent, cribriform pattern with essentially no intervening stroma.
question: Which subtype of endometrial carcinoma does this histology most strongly suggest, and with which risk factor is it classically associated?

options.text: Serous carcinoma, associated with endometrial atrophy
Clear cell carcinoma, associated with diethylstilbestrol exposure
Carcinosarcoma, associated with prior pelvic radiation
Mucinous carcinoma, associated with chronic endometritis
Endometrioid carcinoma, associated with long-term unopposed estrogen

explanation_correct: Endometrioid carcinoma is the most common subtype of endometrial carcinoma. It is associated with long-term exposure to unopposed estrogen (as in obesity, nulliparity, chronic anovulation, HRT, tamoxifen). Its histology is characterized by confluent endometrial glands without intervening stroma. This patient's postmenopausal bleeding, obesity, nulliparity, and glandular histology fit that subtype.

explanation_incorrect.A: Serous carcinoma is a separate, more aggressive subtype associated with endometrial atrophy rather than unopposed estrogen, and it is not defined by confluent glands without stroma.
explanation_incorrect.B: Clear cell carcinoma of the endometrium is not the classic unopposed-estrogen tumor; DES exposure is linked to vaginal clear cell adenocarcinoma, a different site.
explanation_incorrect.C: Carcinosarcoma (malignant mixed Mullerian tumor) is a biphasic epithelial and mesenchymal tumor, not the pure glandular pattern described.
explanation_incorrect.D: Mucinous carcinoma is a rare subtype and is not the classic confluent-gland tumor associated with unopposed estrogen.

educationalObjective: Endometrioid carcinoma is the most common endometrial cancer, linked to unopposed estrogen, with confluent glands lacking intervening stroma.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A medical student is reviewing the epidemiology of gynecologic tumors. She recalls that one benign tumor is the single most common gynecologic neoplasm and occurs with increased frequency in women of African descent.
question: Which of the following tumors fits this description?

options.text: Endometrioid carcinoma of the endometrium
Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia
Leiomyoma (uterine fibroid)
Endometriosis
Adenomyosis

explanation_correct: Leiomyoma (fibroid) is a benign myometrial tumor and is the most common gynecologic tumor overall. It arises during reproductive years, and its incidence is increased in the Black population. It is frequently multiple and can cause abnormal bleeding and pelvic pressure.

explanation_incorrect.A: Endometrioid carcinoma is the most common gynecologic malignancy in resource-rich countries, but it is malignant and not the most common gynecologic tumor overall, nor is it specifically increased in Black women.
explanation_incorrect.B: Endometrial hyperplasia is a premalignant proliferation driven by unopposed estrogen, not the most common gynecologic neoplasm.
explanation_incorrect.D: Endometriosis is ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus; it is not a neoplasm.
explanation_incorrect.E: Adenomyosis is endometrial tissue within the myometrium; it is a benign condition but not a tumor and not the most common gynecologic neoplasm.

educationalObjective: Leiomyoma is the most common gynecologic tumor, occurs in reproductive-age women, and has increased incidence in Black women.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 40-year-old woman with a uterine leiomyoma reports heavy menstrual bleeding. Imaging shows a fibroid that protrudes into and deforms the endometrial cavity.
question: Which subtype of leiomyoma is most likely responsible for her abnormal bleeding?

options.text: Subserosal
Submucosal
Intramural
Pedunculated serosal
Parasitic

explanation_correct: Leiomyomas are classified by location as submucosal (just beneath the endometrium, protruding into the cavity), intramural (within the myometrium), or subserosal (beneath the serosa). Submucosal fibroids are the most likely to cause abnormal uterine bleeding and reproductive dysfunction because they distort the endometrial cavity and interfere with implantation, even when small.

explanation_incorrect.A: Subserosal fibroids grow outward toward the serosa and are less likely to cause bleeding; they more often cause pelvic pressure or are asymptomatic.
explanation_incorrect.C: Intramural fibroids lie within the myometrium; they can cause bleeding when large but are less strongly associated with bleeding than submucosal lesions.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pedunculated serosal fibroids are subserosal tumors on a stalk and typically cause pressure symptoms rather than bleeding.
explanation_incorrect.E: Parasitic fibroids derive a blood supply from other abdominal organs after detaching from the uterus; they are not a standard location subtype linked to bleeding.

educationalObjective: Submucosal leiomyomas most often cause abnormal uterine bleeding and reproductive dysfunction by distorting the endometrial cavity.
